items.title: T3 Code is STEALING Your Data?
items.summary:
Star PandaCode here: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll break down the T3 Code telemetry controversy that followed realchendahuang's viral source code breakdown on X and revisit the reproducible audit I published about a month earlier. I'll trace how default-on telemetry launched on March 6, how the homepage added its opt-in promise on May 14 and removed it on June 18, and how T3 handled requests for a switch. I'll walk through what I found in my audit, which privacy fixes shipped in stable version 0.1.12, why deleted source threads can retain history, and how the mobile trace switch reached phones through a separate over-the-air update. I'll show how PandaCode applies supported opt-out flags when it starts new harness sessions, how PandaCode Connect and thread deletion work, and how PandaCode performed in my benchmarks against T3 Code. I'll close with the desktop teleme
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi, welcome to another video. [music] So, T3 code is in a big telemetry controversy on X this week. It started when Real Chendehuang posted a breakdown of the T3 code source code, and that post went viral with hundreds of thousands of views. I raised this exact issue on X about a month ago, and I published a full reproducible audit and benchmark as the telemetry compare summary inside the Pandacode repository, and anyone can still run the audit. So, let me be clear, I do not think Theo and the T3 code team had bad intent. The code is open source, and their privacy policy now says they collect usage data. In the startup analytics I captured, I saw no emails, prompts, or file contents. But if you care about privacy, what those events did contain matters. First, let's walk through what actually happened in the T3 code repository and where things went wrong. On March 6, 2026, PR 174 shipped post hoc telemetry. The T3 code telemetry setting turned it on by default. For more than 3 months, the homepage still said no telemetry unless you opt in. Full stop. Theo deleted those lines in a June 18th commit during a homepage redesign in PR 3137. Existing users got no notice. In issue 1397, a user asked for an opt-out setting. On June 23, maintainer Julius closed it as not planned and wrote, we will not make this easier to opt out of. It is crucial for us to know how many users we have. On July 18th, issue 4123 called out the gap between that promise and default on telemetry. Theo closed it in October, reopened it the next day, and closed it again on November 4th, still with no in-app switch. On October 18th, PR 15028 moved telemetry to T3's own endpoint ingest.t3.codes. T3 code flushes a batch every 10 seconds. The endpoint archives the raw events and forwards them to post hoc. When the change merged, post hoc still got every event. On November 17th, Julius closed PR 27077, a community proposal a full opt-out toggle with 107 passing tests. He said it is not something the project wants to take on. Earlier opt-out PRs hit PR size limits or their authors closed them. Then on November 23 PR dropped the model name filter. Until the next day's patch, analytics sent unknown model IDs as entered including custom models and models served by a custom endpoint. Now the part that crosses the line for me is how T3 code identifies users and this is what I tested myself last month. The file behind this was identified.ts. It shipped on March 6 in PR 174. It read your Codex sign in file and hashed your account ID with SHA 256. On March 20th PR 124 it read your Codex sign in file and hashed your account ID with SHA 256. On March 20th PR 1249 added your Claude user ID. PR 21506 opened on October 19th and merged the next day. It added an owner tracking event which tied hashed account IDs to the same installation. Until the November 24 patch the analytics code read the Codex and Claude sign in files from your home folder. In the build I tested it hashed your Codex workspace ID, OpenAI user ID, and Claude account UUID separately without assault. If you use T3 Connect it could link that account to the same install ID too. An unsalted SHA 256 hash of a stable account ID is pseudonymous. Anyone who knows the original ID can compute the same hash and match it to the analytics. A ChatGPT team admin could match the workspace ID and T3 can match IDs for its own connect accounts. Under GDPR and CCPA persistent identifiers can count as personal data when they can be linked to a person. In my own test I put fake Canary emails, usernames, and tokens in test login files. I sent the startup analytics to a local collector. None of those fake values appeared in the analytics payloads and I saw no prompts or file contents there. The idle test could see traffic to Axiom but I could not read those encrypted traces. T3 code also set the post-hog person profile flagged to false, credit where it is due. The bad news is the idle test. In five out of five fresh launches with no sign-in and no clicks, T3 code sent about 3.3 kilobytes per run to the shared ingest and relay address. It also sent about 18 kilobytes per run to axiom. In that build, the boot heartbeat fired before you could act on the welcome screen. Axiom traffic went out even with T3 connect off. Before the November 24 patches, the mobile app had no switch for connection traces. On desktop, the documented opt-out still uses an environment variable. On Mac or Linux, set the T3 code telemetry variable to false in your shell profile and restart the app. On Windows, set it as a user environment variable. The open telemetry disable flag can also stop trace exports. As of version 0.112 PR 42629 also makes T3 code respect the standard do not track variable, and it wins over the T3 code telemetry flag. PR 42630 turns telemetry off by default on CI runners, but both still rely on environment variables, not an in-app switch. Two more real issues came up too, the database bug and the questions around T3 connect. In issue 178045 opened in October, deleting a thread only set a deleted timestamp in the local database, so the rows stayed. Some users reported databases between 25 and 62 gigabytes, even though the pop-up said it permanently clears the thread. And T3's own FAQ says T3 connect rides a Cloudflare tunnel. That FAQ does not document any end-to-end encryption on top of the tunnel. T3 moved fast on November 24th. They merged a fix that stops analytics from reading Codex and Claude sign-in files or sending hashed OpenAI and Claude IDs. Another fix replaces unknown model names in analytics with a custom label for the provider. They added a mobile switch for connection traces and removed the install ID from agent feedback. They also stopped recording IP addresses and user agents in relay traces. Then on November 25th, PR 42119 closed issue 17845. Deleting a thread now purges its conversation history while a tombstone and some metadata stay behind. And credit to T3 here. All of these privacy fixes plus the do not track and CI changes shipped in stable version 0.112 on November 25th. You do not need a nightly build to get them. So as of November 25th, here is what T3 still collects. Desktop analytics still sends a hashed install ID, client device links, and a link to your T3 connect account if you use it. Desktop telemetry is still on by default and there is still no in-app opt-out toggle. The Windows fix only makes the app honor the existing environment variable. So if you want a multi-agent coding app built for privacy from day one, let me show you how Pandacode handles all of this. Pandacode is free and open source. It uses the MIT-based Pandacode license and the only ask is that you credit Pandacode if you fork it. First, Pandacode has zero telemetry by default. There is no post hog, no axiom, no century, and no open telemetry anywhere in its dependency manifests. The app Windows content security policy allows only local app IPC connections. Network requests go through Rust. In the same five-run idle benchmark, Pandacode contacted zero analytics hosts. Now here is exactly what Pandacode does contact. It checks GitHub releases for app updates which you can turn off in settings about update mode. It checks the versions of your installed agent CLIs and that check has no off switch yet. It runs GH auth status if you enable GitHub integration. And it gets a public price list once a day when you open the usage view. And yes, the usage view also reads your local CLI credentials. It only uses them to ask your own vendor for your own plan limits. It never hashes them and it never sends them to any Pandacode server. Then there is the one-click option to turn off agent telemetry. In settings, agents, harnesses, advanced privacy, you flip one switch. Pandacode automatically passes the standard do not track flag to every coding harness along with each agent's own opt-out. That includes disabling telemetry and Claude code and anti-gravity and turning off Codex analytics. It also covers Kimi, Grok, DeepSeek, Open Code, and Pi. It never changes your config files. Now, privacy is not only about turning off analytics, it is also about remote access and local data. Panda Code Connect is off until you opt in. It connects up to 10 machines with real end-to-end encryption. It uses X 25519 for key exchange, HKDF SHA 256 to derive keys, and X ChaCha20 Poly1305 to encrypt messages. Every new device or changed key stays pending until you approve it locally with view only, control, or full access. The Cloudflare worker relay only forwards encrypted blobs and stores zero task tech. Thread deletion is also real. When you delete a thread in Panda Code, it runs a real SQL delete in SQLite. That delete cascades across messages, workers, and turn changes. So, deleted threads never pile up as hidden rows in your database. For Google anti-gravity, Panda Code runs Google's official AG CLI over ACP. There is no private API and no header spoofing. Now, the benchmark numbers from the same summary. These measurements are from Panda Code version 0.3.79 compared against the October 26 T3 code nightly build. Panda Code uses Tauri 2, Rust, and the native OS web view, while T3 code ships Electron on disk. Panda Code is 48.6 MB and T3 code is 456.5 MB that makes Panda Code more than nine times smaller. Time to first window is 740 ms against 2,906 ms which is nearly four times faster. Idle memory is 418 MB against 633 MB and Panda Code runs 43 threads against 140. One honest caveat here. Total CPU in the first minute was higher on Panda Code at 10.3 seconds against 7.4 seconds. That is because Panda code runs a version check on each CLI at launch. Its own process is used less than half the CPU at 3.2 seconds against 7.0 seconds. And the best part is that you do not give up features to get this privacy. In Panda code version 0.345 you get 21 coding harnesses including Claude code, Codex, Anti Gravity, Kimmy, Open Code, GLM, Deep Seek, Grok, and more. You also get agent teams, Panda router, council review, bots for Telegram, Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp, local tart VMs, a built-in browser, and Git work trees. Version 0.3436 came out on November 25 and adds optional browser access to your session. It stays on your own machine by default and uses plain HTTP there. So the end-to-end encryption I mentioned covers Panda code connect, not this local browser mode. Now the caveats. The Mac OS builds are signed and notarized, but the Windows installers can still trigger a smart screen warning the first time you run them. The CLI version checks still need a toggle and Panda code relies on the CLIs that you already install. So here is my verdict. I still do not think Theo had bad intent with T3 code and credit to the team for fixing thread deletion and shipping these privacy fixes in a stable release. One ask remains. Desktop telemetry is still on by default with no in-app opt-out toggle in the settings. Even the open community PR 42625 which adds a settings toggle would still default to on. Give desktop users a real switch or make telemetry opt-in by default. That one change would win back a lot of trust. Until then, if you want a fast open source multi-agent workspace, Panda code is the best option right now. You get zero telemetry by default, one click agent opt-outs, and end-to-end encrypted remote access with Panda code connect. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the [music] super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs [music] up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
